items.scenario: You ask Claude to summarise a 40-message migration thread into a paragraph plus an action table. The table lists 'Owner: Ravi, Due: Friday' for the DNS cutover. You don't remember Ravi agreeing to anything.
items.question: What is the most likely explanation, and the right next step?
options: Claude likely caught a message you skimmed past; post the table exactly as written
The Owner/Due columns invited a guess; find the source message or mark it UNASSIGNED
Ravi owns DNS on this team, so the inference is sound; keep that row and post the table
Regenerate the summary twice more and keep whichever owner appears most often
items.explanation: A table format with Owner and Due columns pressures the model to fill every cell, so invented owners and dates are a known summarisation failure. Ask for a source citation per action and an explicit UNASSIGNED / NO DATE when nobody committed, then check against the thread.
distractors: Possible, but unverified. Posting it assigns work to someone who may never have agreed to it.
Owning an area is not agreeing to a task. Inferring owners is exactly the error to avoid.
Re-sampling measures consistency, not truth. Only the thread can settle who agreed.

items.scenario: During a SEV-2 checkout outage you need a public status-page update and an exec update. You have confirmed impact, start time and current mitigation, but no root cause yet.
items.question: How should you use Claude?
options: One update for both audiences, adding the likely root cause so customers feel reassured early
Confirmed facts only; two drafts: customer (impact, next update) and exec (risk, decision)
Paste the whole incident channel and let Claude decide which details are safe to publish
Hold all communication until the root cause is confirmed, then draft both updates at once
items.explanation: Same facts, different readers: pick the register on purpose. Supply only confirmed facts. A speculative root cause on a public page is a commitment you may have to retract.
distractors: One register fails both readers, and public root-cause speculation is a claim you can't yet back.
Over-shares internal context (names, speculation, maybe customer data) and hands the public/private judgement to the model.
Stakeholders need updates during the incident. Silence until root cause is a communication failure.

items.scenario: You have a 30-page project report and 20 minutes to present its outcome to a steering committee next week.
items.question: What is the best first request to Claude?
options: 'Turn this report into a 10-slide deck', then rework whichever slides look the weakest
'Write the story in six sentences: situation, problem, result, ask', then outline slides
'Give me one slide per report section', so the deck mirrors the document faithfully
'Pick a professional template and fill it from the report', then rehearse with speaker notes
items.explanation: Narrative before slides: agree the storyline first, then cut it into a deck outline (one takeaway per slide title, speaker notes carrying detail). The slide tool only renders structure; it doesn't create it.
distractors: Generating slides first locks in a structure nobody chose; you end up polishing slides with no argument.
A report's section order serves a reader, not a 20-minute audience that needs the outcome and the ask.
Templates fix appearance, not narrative. The committee needs a storyline and a clear ask.

items.scenario: You need a 12-page runbook for a new service. A colleague suggests asking Claude to 'write the full runbook' in one prompt to save time.
items.question: Which approach produces the most reliable document?
options: One prompt for the full runbook, then a careful single read-through before publishing
Approve an outline, draft section by section, then run a consistency and glossary pass
Generate three complete drafts in separate chats and merge the strongest paragraphs
Write the runbook by hand, since Claude loses track of anything longer than a page
items.explanation: Outline-first fixes the argument cheaply, section-level drafting limits drift, and a consistency/glossary pass catches contradictions in terms and numbers.
distractors: Long one-shot output drifts and is hard to review thoroughly in one pass.
Three independent drafts multiply inconsistency in terms and numbers rather than removing it.
Over-correction: long documents work well with the structured approach.

items.scenario: Claude's drafts of your weekly engineering updates are fine but don't sound like you; teammates can tell. You have a year of your own updates in a folder.
items.question: What is the most effective fix?
options: Add 'write exactly like me, casual but precise' to the top of every request
Build a custom Style from three of your own updates and apply it to these drafts
Paste a different old update into each chat and ask Claude to copy its wording
Upload the whole year of updates into every chat so Claude can learn your voice from them
items.explanation: A custom Style built from samples of the same genre conditions every draft on your patterns without re-explaining each time. A few representative samples beat adjectives or bulk uploads.
distractors: Adjectives like 'casual but precise' are vague; samples show the model what you mean.
Copying one sample invites reused phrasing and drifts between chats; a Style is consistent and reusable.
Bulk uploads waste context and share far more than the task needs; a few good samples suffice.

items.scenario: A draft proposal has good sentences, but the argument is in the wrong order and the cost section is missing. A teammate has started line-editing it with Claude.
items.question: What should happen first?
options: Finish the line edits so the prose is clean, then sort out structure
Ask for a structural critique without rewriting, fix it, then line-edit
Have Claude add a cost section at the end and keep the current order
Ask Claude to rewrite the entire proposal from scratch in a fresh chat
items.explanation: Structural edits come before line edits. Polishing paragraphs that will be moved or cut wastes effort, and a critique-without-rewrite keeps the author's material and intent.
distractors: Polished sentences get cut or moved when the structure changes, so the work is wasted.
Patches the gap but leaves the argument in the wrong order, which was the main problem.
Discards the good material and the author's intent without diagnosing what was wrong.

items.scenario: Your six-person delivery team writes client emails daily and keeps getting product names, sign-offs and banned phrases inconsistent.
items.question: What is the most durable way to get consistency with Claude?
options: Each person pastes the house rules into a chat whenever they remember to
Put the voice guide and glossary in a shared Project's instructions
Ask Claude in one chat to remember the house rules for everyone
Circulate one approved email that everyone uses as a fixed template
items.explanation: Project instructions apply to every chat in the Project without anyone remembering to add them, so the whole team drafts from the same rules.
distractors: Relying on memory means the rules are forgotten or applied inconsistently.
One chat's context doesn't carry to teammates' chats.
A single template covers one situation; a voice guide generalises across emails.

items.scenario: You ask Claude to summarise a private incident-review DM thread, which names a customer and an engineer's mistake, and post the summary in the public #engineering channel.
items.question: What is the main problem?
options: The summary will be too long to read comfortably in a busy channel
Posting it publicly discloses private content to the whole channel
The summary will lose nuance, so it should go in a thread reply
Claude should post it from a bot account rather than under your name
items.explanation: Visibility and etiquette: assume everyone in the channel sees what's posted. M8.1's rules apply to a summary just as they apply to the original.
distractors: Length is a style issue; the audience mismatch is the real problem.
A thread reply is still visible to the whole channel; it doesn't fix the disclosure.
Changing the poster doesn't change who can read it; the content is the problem.

items.scenario: Claude produces release notes from 60 commits. They read beautifully. Your reviewer approves after a skim, and the notes describe an internal refactor as a new user-facing feature.
items.question: Which practice would most reliably have prevented this?
options: A second reviewer reading the finished notes end to end for clarity
A commit hash per line, checked against the diff in a separate pass
Asking Claude to double-check its own notes before handing them over
Generating the notes at a higher effort level with a stronger model
items.explanation: Fluent isn't correct, and polished text lowers vigilance. Traceability (a citation per line) plus a deliberate verification pass, separate from reading for flow, catches mis-categorised changes.
distractors: Another read for flow repeats the same blind spot; verification needs a different method.
Self-review by the same model isn't independent; it tends to confirm its own framing.
More capability reduces errors but doesn't remove the need to verify against the source.

items.scenario: You correspond in English with a Japanese client about a contract change. You draft in English and want to send in Japanese.
items.question: What is the safest workflow?
options: Ask Claude for a polite Japanese version and send it, since its translation is reliable
Get the Japanese and a back-translation, check meaning, have a fluent colleague review
Send the English only and let the client run it through their own translation tools
Send the Japanese and English side by side, unreviewed, so the client can compare them
items.explanation: Multi-language drafting is a strength, but contractual terms need human verification. A back-translation exposes meaning drift you can check yourself; a fluent reviewer covers register and legal wording.
distractors: Register, honorifics and legal terms are exactly where unchecked translation fails.
Pushes the risk onto the client's tools, which you can't check either.
Two unreviewed versions may disagree, and you've created two documents with contractual weight.
